implementation_notes: Go's standard library ships no striped container, so the idiom is hand-written: a fixed array of sync.RWMutex values, one per shard, each shard holding its own map, plus a stable hash reduced modulo the shard count (use a power-of-two shard count to replace the modulo with a mask). Reads take RLock/RUnlock and writes Lock/Unlock. sync.Map is the standard library's concurrent map, but its documentation scopes it to append-only caches and disjoint-key workloads, so it is an alternative for those cases rather than a general striping replacement.
pitfalls: A sync.RWMutex must not be copied after first use: keep the shards in a slice or array inside the owner and expose methods on a pointer receiver (go vet's copylocks check catches the common mistakes).
A nil map in a shard panics on write; initialize every shard before serving, and remember that iterating shards yields a per-shard snapshot, not a consistent view of the whole store.

sync.Map is not a drop-in replacement: its documentation excludes workloads with frequent overlapping writes of the same key, which is precisely where a striped map with per-key compound operations is needed.
